newsitem.title: TANZANIA: South African delegation arrives in Tanzania.
newsitem.headline: South African delegation arrives in Tanzania.

text.p: A South African delegation including senior military officers arrived in Tanzania on Thursday to assess how Pretoria could contribute to ending disaster in Zaire.
"It's a first, very hesitant and investigative step from South Africa before involvement in the region. It's definitely not a military planning excercise," Colonel Tienie van Schalkwyk told Reuters.

Schalkwyk said the delegation's purpose was a fact finding mission and a follow up to last week's meeting between President Nelson Mandela and former Tanzanian president Julius Nyerere, the international mediator for the Great Lakes region.
Mandela said on Wednesday the team in Tanzania would consider military questions and political solutions to the crisis and would find out exactly what was required of South Africa.
The president earlier said he was prepared to send troops to Central Africa as part of an international intervention force, but needed more information to decide how many to commit.

Schalkwyk, defence attache at the South African embassy in Dar es Salaam, said the team, on a two-day visit, was led by Rusty Evans, director-general of the South African foreign ministry and included three senior military officers.
The senior officer is Lieutenant-General Wessel Kritzinger, chief of staff for defence operations.
The delegation was scheduled to meet with Nyerere later on Thursday before lunch with Tanzanian foreign ministry officials.
Schalkwyk said many issues needed to be resolved before South African troops could be deployed as part of a multinational force in eastern Zaire.
He said it was unlikely South Africa would commit combat troops but would rather play a key supporting role possibly involved in logistics, communications, field engineers or the medical field.
U.N. Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali says he expects more than 12 countries to provide troops and equipment for the force to open up aid routes to Rwandan and Burundian refugees in Zaire.
The United States and Britain said on Wednesday they were prepared to contribute troops to a multinational force in Zaire. France, Spain and other countries have said they are ready to join it.
